text: The multi-billion rupee Gurgaon kidney scandal was exposed in January 2008 when police conducted raids on a residential building and a guest house owned by Amit Kumar in Gurgaon, an industrial township near New Delhi, India. The victims, mostly poor individuals from western Uttar Pradesh, including Moradabad, were lured with promises of job opportunities and offered about Rs. 30,000 for kidney 'donation'. Those who refused were drugged and operated on against their will. The racket, which had been ongoing for six to seven years, involved the transplantation of kidneys from these donors into clients from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Saudi Arabia, and Greece. The Haryana police issued arrest warrants against Upendra Aggarwal, a general physician and associate of Amit Kumar, and the raid rescued five people, who were shifted to a Gurgaon hospital. On 25 January 2008, U.S.-based non-resident Indian couple and three Greek nationals, two of whom were transplant patients, were detained. Police revealed that Dr. Amit Kumar and his accomplices had performed 600 kidney transplants over the past decade, with at least two hospitals involved in post-transplant care. Fingerprinting evidence showed Kumar used multiple aliases and had been previously arrested at least four times for illegal organ trade, with prior arrests in Delhi, Andhra Pradesh, and Maharashtra involving Kumar, his brother Jeevan Kumar, Upendra Aggarwal, and Saraj Kumar, all of whom were released on bail. On 7 January 2008, Kumar was arrested by Delhi Police but released after a bribe of Rs. 20 lakhs; Jeevan Kumar was arrested on 17 February 2008 in Delhi. The Indian Medical Association requested a probe by its three-member committee and a further investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). Haryana police also uncovered two hospitals and ten laboratories in Greater Noida and Meerut allegedly involved in the scandal. As suspicions grew that Kumar had fled, the Haryana police requested CBI to alert Interpol, leading to red corner notices for Kumar and his brother. On 7 February 2008, Amit Kumar was arrested in Nepal, hiding in a wildlife resort about 35 miles from the Indo-Nepal border, where he had Rs. 9,36,000 in bank draft and €145,000 and $18,900 in cash. He attempted to bribe Nepali police to escape but failed. The CBI filed charges against him under sections 326, 342, 420, and 120B. In March 2013, a CBI special court convicted five accused, including Dr. Upender Dublesh and Dr. Amit Kumar, who received seven-year rigorous imprisonment and fines of over Rs. 60 lakh each, with the latter being termed a 'quack' by the court.
